observed_evidence: Reuters reported Saudi Arabia suspended crude loadings at Yanbu and informed European customers that some late-September cargoes would be cancelled after damage to the East-West Pipeline.
Reuters reported Brent settled September 15 at $108.75/bbl and WTI at $105.83/bbl, both highest since May 19.
Reuters reported some European physical crude cargoes traded above $130/bbl as buyers sought alternatives to disrupted Middle East supplies.

Libya's NOC said Hamada, Tahara and NC5 production was halted after the Petroleum Facilities Guard closed a pipeline valve; national output remained about 1.4 million bpd at the time and NOC warned force majeure was possible if disruption spread.

U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the Saudi East-West Pipeline should return within days, but Reuters also cited sources estimating repairs could take longer; restoration timing remains uncertain.
semantic_interpretation: The Saudi shock has progressed from infrastructure damage to confirmed export-cargo cancellation and suspension of Yanbu loadings, while Libya adds a separate supply-risk channel. The physical-market premium above futures indicates acute near-term scarcity. This increases energy-cost, freight, inflation and global-rate pressure relevant to Taiwan equities, although the U.S. statement that the Saudi pipeline may return within days is a meaningful de-escalation scenario that prevents treating the disruption as permanently lost supply.
